headline: DHS Final Rule Permanently Ends Automatic Work Permit Extensions For Renewals
subheadline: The October 14, 2026 rule makes permanent the loss of the 540-day EAD bridge for renewals filed on or after October 30, 2025, hitting H-4 spouses and green card applicants who must now get approval before their card expires.
body:
• DHS published a final rule on October 14, 2026 making permanent the end of the 540-day automatic extension for EAD renewals filed on or after October 30, 2025 — a timely Form I-765 receipt no longer extends work authorization.
  • H-4 spouses in category (c)(26) and adjustment-of-status applicants in (c)(9) are among those affected: if your current EAD expires before USCIS approves the renewal, you generally must stop working until the new card is approved.
  • Renewals filed before October 30, 2025 that qualified keep their automatic extension; E and L spouses authorized incident to status and F-1 STEM OPT holders under their separate 180-day mechanism are not affected in the same way.
  • Action step: file renewals as early as USCIS allows — up to 180 days before expiration — and track the card’s printed expiration date, not the pending receipt, with your employer’s I-9 process.

The Department of Homeland Security has finalized a rule that permanently ends automatic extensions of work permits for many immigrants renewing an Employment Authorization Document, closing the safety net that allowed H-4 spouses and green card applicants to keep working for up to 540 days while U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services processed a timely renewal.

The final rule, published in the Federal Register on October 14, 2026 at 91 Fed. Reg. 65306 (FR Doc. 2026-20955), adopts without substantive change an interim final rule first issued on October 30, 2025. It is effective immediately. DHS said the change “enhances benefit integrity and prioritises the proper vetting and screening of aliens before granting a new period of employment authorization.” USCIS has archived its earlier guidance on the automatic EAD extension page.

Who loses the automatic extension

For renewal applications filed on or after October 30, 2025, filing Form I-765 on time no longer extends an expiring EAD. Work authorization generally ends on the date printed on the current card unless USCIS has approved the renewal or the worker has an independent basis to work.

https://x.com/randyferrell/status/2112334849579073605

The categories that lose the extension include adjustment-of-status applicants, category (c)(9); H-4 spouses, category (c)(26); asylum applicants, category (c)(8); refugees and asylees, categories (a)(3) and (a)(5); and Temporary Protected Status beneficiaries, categories (a)(12) and (c)(19), subject to any separate TPS-specific Federal Register notices.

Three groups are not affected in the same way: renewals filed before October 30, 2025 that qualified for the prior extension; E and L spouses, who remain employment-authorized incident to status; and F-1 STEM OPT students, who continue under a separate 180-day automatic extension mechanism. STEM OPT and cap-gap extensions were also noted as unaffected in broader reporting on the rule.

Why this hits Indian families hardest

H-4 spouses are the dependents of H-1B workers, and adjustment applicants in category (c)(9) are largely people with a pending Form I-485 green card application. Indians make up a disproportionate share of both groups because the per-country cap on employment-based green cards leaves Indian applicants waiting far longer than most other nationalities, spending more years renewing EADs while they wait.

Under the old system, that wait was buffered: a timely renewal could keep a worker employed for up to 540 days. Without it, a USCIS delay becomes a job interruption. Employers, in turn, face I-9 reverification pressure and may have to pause or end employment when a card lapses, even if the worker remains eligible and the renewal is later approved.

In a separate development mentioned briefly for context, 63 members of Congress led by Representatives Yvette Clarke and Raul Grijalva have urged USCIS to accelerate green card processing, citing lawfully present immigrants losing health coverage during delays. That letter does not change the EAD rule, but it underlines why processing speed now matters more: there is no automatic bridge while a case is pending.

What EAD holders should do now

File as early as the rules allow and do not rely on a receipt notice. Workers who depend on an EAD should calendar the printed expiration date, file the renewal up to 180 days in advance where eligible, and talk to immigration counsel and their employer well before expiry about contingency plans if approval has not arrived.

The final rule removes the remaining uncertainty about a policy that has applied since October 2025: it is now permanent unless changed by a future rulemaking or a court order. For Indian H-4 spouses and green card applicants, the practical change is stark — continued employment now depends on USCIS approving the renewal before the current card expires.
